last_assistant_message:
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of every visible color, each with its own wavelength. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it runs into nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are far smaller than those wavelengths. These tiny particles scatter light through a process called Rayleigh scattering, and its strength depends heavily on wavelength: shorter wavelengths scatter far more than longer ones. Blue light scatters about five times more than red, so it gets bounced around the whole sky and reaches your eyes from every direction.

Violet light scatters even more than blue, so you might expect a violet sky. But sunlight contains less violet to begin with, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue. Together, these effects make the sky look blue to us.

The same physics explains why the sky is not equally blue everywhere. Straight overhead, the light reaching you has crossed the least air, so it is a deep, saturated blue. Near the horizon it has crossed far more air, and the scattered blue light is itself scattered again, mixed with light of every color and diluted, so the sky fades to a pale blue or nearly white. On a clear day at high altitude, with less air above you, the sky looks darker and bluer still, and from orbit, with no air at all, it is black.

Clouds look white for a different reason. Their water droplets are much larger than the wavelengths of visible light, so they scatter every color about equally, through a process called Mie scattering: white light in, white light out. A thick cloud looks gray only because less light makes it through to its underside.

At sunrise and sunset, the sun sits low on the horizon, so its light passes through much more atmosphere to reach you. Along that long path, most of the blue and green light gets scattered away. Mostly the longer oranges and reds remain, which paints the sun and nearby clouds in warm colors. Dust, smoke, and other particles in the air can make these colors even stronger.
